pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Water-cycle vocabulary (evaporation, condensation, precipitation…)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science, Year 4 States of matter):** Pupils identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature — using the correct technical vocabulary.

- **Standards — US (NGSS supports 2-ESS2/5-ESS2 & MS-ESS2-4 water-cycle strand):** Name and use water-cycle terms and sequence the stages correctly.

- **Operational details:** This is a LANGUAGE node: the goal is precise, correctly-sequenced vocabulary — evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection/runoff, transpiration, water vapour, groundwater. Each term must be pinned to WHERE it happens and WHAT is changing state: evaporation = liquid→vapour (rising from oceans/lakes, faster when warmer); condensation = vapour→liquid (cooling high up, forming clouds); precipitation = water falling as rain/snow/hail; collection/runoff/groundwater = water gathering and returning. Teach the terms ON a cyclic diagram so 'in the correct sequence' is embodied, and pair each new word with the everyday phenomenon (steam off a puddle, mist on a cold window). The cycle has no start or end — stress the loop.
bestPractices: Attach each term to the state change and the location where it happens (evaporation at warm surfaces, condensation where air cools), not just a definition.
Teach the words ON a labelled cyclic diagram and have children sequence/relabel it so 'correct order' is embodied.
Pair every new term with a concrete everyday observation: steam off a warm puddle (evaporation), droplets on a cold glass (condensation), rain/snow (precipitation).
Contrast the confusable pair evaporation vs condensation directly — opposite directions of the same state change.
Stress that the cycle is a loop with no beginning or end; the Sun is the energy driver.
keyRepresentations: A labelled cyclic water-cycle diagram with arrows (Sun → evaporation → condensation/cloud → precipitation → collection).
A sequencing strip of the stages to order correctly.
A cold-glass / boiling-kettle demonstration linking evaporation and condensation to the words.
commonMisconceptions: Swapping 'evaporation' and 'condensation' — confusing the two opposite directions of state change.
'Clouds are made of water vapour' — clouds are condensed tiny liquid droplets, not invisible vapour.
'The water cycle has a start and an end' — not seeing it as a continuous loop.
'Evaporated water disappears / is used up' — not realising it becomes invisible water vapour still present in the air.
'Precipitation only means rain' — forgetting snow, hail and sleet are precipitation too.
'Rain comes from clouds getting heavy with vapour' — missing that droplets must condense and coalesce first.

learn.summary: Water-cycle vocabulary for ages 7–9: teach the terms evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection/runoff, transpiration, water vapour and groundwater by pinning each to WHERE it happens and, for the terms that involve one (evaporation, condensation, transpiration), WHAT change of state is occurring. Precipitation, collection/runoff and groundwater describe water moving or being stored, not a change of state. The terms are arranged on a cyclic diagram so the correct sequence can be seen. The core teaching move is placing the easily confused pair evaporation and condensation on opposite arrows of the same loop (the same state change, in opposite directions). Every term is paired with a concrete everyday observation, and the cycle is stressed as a continuous loop with no start or end, driven by the Sun's energy.

activities.title: Label and explore a cyclic water-cycle landscape
feedback: When comparing evaporation and condensation, highlight that they sit on opposite arrows of the SAME loop: both are the same state change (liquid↔vapour) but in opposite directions — up and drying versus forming droplets.
If a learner calls the cloud 'water vapour', clarify that the cloud is condensed tiny liquid droplets; the vapour was invisible before it cooled.
If a learner looks for where the cycle 'starts', point back to the ring: any point leads round to itself, so there is no true start or end.
activities.rationale: Attaching each term to its location (and, where one occurs, its state change), teaching the words on a labelled cyclic diagram, and directly contrasting evaporation with condensation targets the most common confusion (swapping the two) by using position on the loop as the anchor.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 4 States of matter: pupils identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature.
Common water-cycle misconceptions: clouds are water vapour (they are condensed droplets); evaporated water 'disappears'; the cycle has a start/end.
learnerActions: Study a labelled cyclic diagram of a landscape: Sun, a lake or puddle, upward arrows showing invisible water vapour rising, a cloud, falling rain, a river, trees, and hidden groundwater below the surface, with arrows forming a ring.
Point to (or on screen, tap) the sun-warmed lake and read/say: 'evaporation — liquid water turns into invisible water vapour, and it happens faster when it is warmer.'
Point to the cloud and read/say: 'condensation — water vapour cools and turns back into tiny liquid droplets that make the cloud.'
Point to the falling rain and say: 'precipitation — water falling as rain, snow, hail or sleet.'
Point to the trees/plants and name 'transpiration' — plants draw up liquid water and release it from their leaves as water vapour (a liquid-to-vapour change, like evaporation but from the plant).

Point to the river and underground layer and name 'collection / runoff' (water gathering and flowing downhill) and 'groundwater' (water that has soaked into the ground and is stored in soil and rock underground).
Trace the ring all the way round, noticing it has no beginning and no end, and that the Sun is the energy that drives it.
activities.intendedInsight: Each water-cycle term names something that happens to water at a specific place: a change of state (evaporation, condensation, transpiration), or water falling, flowing or being stored (precipitation, runoff/collection, groundwater). The stages form a continuous loop driven by the Sun, so 'in the correct sequence' is something you can see in the ring itself.

activities.title: Match each term to an everyday observation
feedback: If a learner limits 'precipitation' to rain, show the snow/hail/sleet pictures and confirm that all water falling from clouds counts, whether liquid or frozen.
If a learner treats evaporated water as 'gone', name the invisible water vapour: it is still water, just in gas form spread in the air.
activities.rationale: Pairing every new term with a concrete everyday observation builds meaning beyond definitions and pre-empts the 'precipitation = rain only' and 'water disappears' misconceptions. (A sorting/matching task can check and reinforce this classification but does not by itself elicit spoken explanation — ask the learner to say why each pairing fits.)
sourceClaims: Common water-cycle misconceptions: clouds are water vapour (they are condensed droplets); evaporated water 'disappears'; the cycle has a start/end.
learnerActions: Match word cards to picture/phenomenon cards: 'evaporation' ↔ a puddle drying up in the sunshine (or wet washing drying on a line); 'condensation' ↔ droplets forming on a cold glass or misted window; 'precipitation' ↔ rain, snow and hail falling.
Say aloud why each pairing fits, naming the state change (e.g. 'the puddle water turns to vapour, so that's evaporation').
Sort pictures of rain, snow, hail and sleet together under 'precipitation' to see it means more than just rain.
activities.intendedInsight: Each technical word describes something children can actually observe, and precipitation covers snow, hail and sleet, not only rain.

activities.title: Sequence the stages and complete the cycle in words
feedback: If stages are ordered correctly but the learner thinks the sequence ends, remind them the last stage feeds back into evaporation — close the loop.
If evaporation and condensation are swapped in the cloze, re-anchor: evaporation = liquid → vapour (going up, drying); condensation = vapour → liquid (droplets/cloud forming).
Reward completing the described cycle with the right terms rather than memorised definitions.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, cloze completion and term–definition matching directly check correct and correctly-ordered use against the objective; distinguishing evaporation from condensation in context targets the key misconception. These recognition/placement checks confirm ordering but do not by themselves show independent production.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 Year 4 States of matter: pupils identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature.
learnerActions: Order a set of stage strips into the cycle: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection/runoff, then note the loop returns to evaporation.
Complete a short cloze paragraph describing a water-cycle journey by writing the correct term in each blank.

Match each term to its definition, and choose the correct word to distinguish evaporation from condensation in a described situation ('water vapour cools high up and forms tiny droplets' → condensation).
activities.intendedInsight: Correct use of the vocabulary means placing each term in its right slot within a real journey, not just reciting a definition.

activities.title: Boiling-kettle and cold-plate demonstration
feedback: If the learner says the droplets 'came from the plate', clarify the water came from the vapour in the air condensing onto the cool surface.
Link the demo back to the diagram: the kettle is like the warm lake, the cold plate is like the cool air high up where clouds form.
activities.rationale: A hands-on demonstration gives a concrete, immediate experience of the confusable pair, complementing the labelled diagram; it is offered as a complement, not a replacement for the vocabulary work.
learnerActions: Watch (with adult supervision) water being heated in a kettle. Name the change as evaporation: hot liquid water quickly turns into invisible water vapour (in a boiling kettle this happens very fast, and is called boiling). Notice that the white cloud a little way from the spout is not vapour: the vapour has already cooled and condensed into tiny droplets.
Watch while the adult holds a cold plate or lid in the rising steam, keeping your hands well away, and see droplets form on it. Name this as condensation: vapour cooling back into liquid.
Say both words in a sentence describing what just happened, pointing out they are opposite directions of the same change.
activities.intendedInsight: Evaporation and condensation are two opposite directions of one state change. In a single demonstration you can see the results of both within a few seconds: the water level slowly drops as liquid turns into invisible vapour, and liquid droplets appear where the vapour cools.

activities.title: Tell the story of a raindrop's journey (spoken production)
feedback: If the learner swaps the terms ('the cloud evaporates into rain'), anchor it: evaporation = liquid → vapour (going up, drying); condensation = vapour → liquid (cloud/droplets forming).
If the learner says the water 'disappears' or 'turns into air', name the invisible gas as water vapour — still water, just in gas form.
If the learner over-extends 'precipitation' to any water, don't drill definitions — give more in-context examples (rain, snow, hail are precipitation) and let usage sharpen.
If the learner lists the terms correctly but out of order, ask them to re-tell the story following one water drop, step by step.
activities.rationale: Spoken narration with responsive follow-up prompts elicits independent production and can reveal misuse (such as swapping evaporation and condensation) that a memorised definition or a recognition-only check would hide. Efficacy of this format is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Narrate aloud the journey of water starting from a puddle in the Sun, following it all the way until it could fall as rain again.

Use the proper words in sequence: the Sun heats the puddle so water evaporates into water vapour; the vapour rises, cools and condenses into cloud droplets; the droplets join together and grow heavy enough to fall as precipitation (rain, snow or hail); the water collects and runs off into rivers, or soaks into the ground as groundwater, and the cycle repeats.

Respond to follow-up prompts, for example: 'You said the water went up — what is the proper word for water turning into a gas and rising?'; 'When the cloud droplets form, is that evaporation or condensation? Use the word in a sentence.'; 'Where does groundwater fit in your story?'; 'If rain lands on a hill and flows downhill into a river, what do we call that?'
activities.intendedInsight: Genuine command of the vocabulary shows up when each term is used correctly in its right slot within a self-produced narrative, not when definitions are recited in isolation.

constraints: This is a language/vocabulary objective: the goal is precise, correctly-sequenced terminology (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection/runoff, transpiration, water vapour, groundwater), each pinned to its location and, where one occurs, its state change.

Matching, ordering and multiple-choice checks assess recognition and placement; they do not by themselves show the learner can independently produce the vocabulary in a connected narrative — include a spoken (or written) retelling for that.
The boiling-kettle demonstration requires adult supervision for safety and is a complement to, not a substitute for, naming the terms on the diagram.

A drag-the-labels or droplet-journey animation can add engagement, but the learning payload here is naming and sequencing, which does not require any live recomputation; keep such activities focused on naming each stage encountered.
Confirm at least four terms used correctly and in order, with evaporation distinguished from condensation, before treating the objective as met.
Stress the cycle as a continuous loop with no beginning or end, with the Sun as the energy driver; avoid framing any one stage as the fixed 'start'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their support as unconfirmed.

The original research rated a 3D landscape and an in-role conversation as poor fit and asserted phrasings like '3D adds no vocabulary benefit' and conversation 'has no persona payoff'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources, so they have been dropped rather than asserted; a spoken narration activity is retained because producing the vocabulary aloud is a legitimate production task for a language objective.

The source also frames vocabulary acquisition as 'best via labelled imagery and rehearsal', a comparative-efficacy claim not established by the cited sources; it has not been propagated as a universal law.

The DfE sourceClaim was removed from the spoken-narration activity: the citation supports the objective's content but does not establish that the spoken-production format is necessary, tested or more effective.

Self-audit of science content: evaporation (liquid→vapour) and condensation (vapour→liquid) are correctly described as opposite directions of the same state change; clouds are condensed liquid droplets (not vapour); evaporation rate increases with temperature; precipitation includes rain, snow, hail and sleet; transpiration is liquid water released from plants as vapour. No arithmetic or force/motion content present. No conceptual errors were found in the learner-facing actions.

probeDeeper: You said the water 'went up' — what's the proper word for water turning into a gas and rising?
When the cloud droplets form, is that evaporation or condensation? Use the word in a sentence.
Where does the word 'groundwater' fit in your story?
If the rain lands on a hill and flows downhill into a river, what do we call that?
assess.correctAnswer: The child narrates the cycle using the terms correctly and in sequence: the Sun heats the puddle so the water evaporates into water vapour; the vapour rises, cools and condenses into cloud droplets (condensation); the droplets fall as precipitation (rain, snow or hail); the water collects and runs off (runoff, collection) into rivers and groundwater, and the cycle repeats.

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps 'evaporation' and 'condensation' ('the cloud evaporates into rain')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor it: evaporation = liquid → vapour (going up, drying); condensation = vapour → liquid (cloud/droplets forming).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: uses the wrong term for the direction of the change

errorPatterns.pattern: Says 'the water disappears / turns into air' instead of 'evaporates into water vapour'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the invisible gas as water vapour — still water, just in gas form.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: avoids the term water vapour and treats the water as gone

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-extends 'precipitation' to any water, not just falling rain/snow/hail
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't drill definitions — give more in-context examples (rain, snow, hail are precipitation) and let usage sharpen.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: stretches the newly learned word too widely

errorPatterns.pattern: Recites the terms as a list but out of sequence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-tell the story following one water drop, step by step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: knows the words but jumbles their order in the narrative

responseLevels.gap: Avoids the technical terms or uses them wrongly (swaps evaporation/condensation); says the water 'disappears.'
responseLevels.full: Narrates the water cycle using at least four terms correctly and in the right order, distinguishing evaporation from condensation and using 'water vapour' and 'precipitation' appropriately in context.
responseLevels.partial: Uses some terms correctly but misplaces one or two in the sequence, or lists them without a coherent journey.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell me the story of a raindrop's journey around the water cycle — start with a puddle in the Sun and follow the water all the way until it could fall as rain again. Use the proper words as you go, and I'll listen for how you use them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Using each term correctly in the right slot of a real narrative (evaporation going up, condensation forming cloud, precipitation coming down) shows genuine command, whereas a memorised definition wouldn't reveal a misuse such as swapping evaporation and condensation.
